name: 81-1 ICT1 AC1 MCQ 1
content: What is the smallest single unit that forms a digital image on a computer?
explanation: A pixel is the tiny basic unit that makes up all digital images.

name: Image Resolution
content: An image has a width of 800 pixels and a height of 600 pixels. What is the total number of pixels in this image?
explanation: To calculate the total number of pixels in an image, multiply the width by the height. In this case, 800 pixels (width) × 600 pixels (height) = 480,000 pixels total.

name: Color Depth and Resolution
content: What is the term for the number of distinct colors that can be displayed in a digital image or on a computer display?
explanation: Color depth refers to the number of distinct colors that can be displayed or represented in an image. It is typically measured in bits per pixel (bpp), with higher values allowing for more colors. For example, 8-bit color depth can display 256 colors (2^8), while 24-bit color depth (true color) can display over 16 million colors (2^24). Resolution, on the other hand, refers to the number of pixels displayed on screen, while pixel density relates to the concentration of pixels in a given area. Bit rate is a measure of data transmission speed and not directly related to color representation.

content.text: Arrange the 6 image processing steps in the correct order - from the raw input image to the final image ready for AI.

explanation: Correct order: `Input Image` → `Grayscale` → `Noise Reduction` → `Enhancement` → `Feature Emphasis` → `Processed Image`.

name: P1001 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1001 (Output the Second Variable): read three variables and print only the second one, b. (OJ: P1001 — Output the Second Variable)

explanation: The three input lines must come first and in order: each `input()` reads one value from its own line, so `a`, `b` and `c` are filled exactly as the input format requires. The last line `print(b)` outputs only the second variable read — which is all the task asks for.

name: P1002 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1002 (Print Three Variables on One Line): print a, b and c on a single line separated by spaces. (OJ: P1002 — Print Three Variables on One Line)

explanation: Read `a`, `b` and `c` in the order they appear in the input. Then `print(a, b, c)` writes all three on one line — `print` automatically inserts a space between arguments, which is exactly the required single-line, space-separated format. The print must come after all three variables exist.

name: P1003 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1003 (Print Hi): print "Hi " followed by the string s. (OJ: P1003 — Print Hi)

explanation: Read the string first with `s = input()`. The print line glues the greeting onto the user text with string concatenation: `"Hi " + s` — the trailing space inside the quotes separates `Hi` from the name. Printing before `s` exists would crash, so the print goes last.

name: P1004 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1004 (Addition and Subtraction): read two integers and print their sum on the first line and their difference on the second line. (OJ: P1004 — Addition and Subtraction)

explanation: Read `a` and `b` first — both must exist before any computing. Then `print(a + b)` writes the sum on the first line and `print(a - b)` writes the difference on the second. Each `print` ends its own line, so two print calls in the right order produce the two required output lines.

name: P1005 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1005 (Multiplication and Division): read two integers and print their product on the first line and their quotient on the second line. (OJ: P1005 — Multiplication and Division)

explanation: Read `a` and `b`, then print the product `a * b` first and the quotient `a / b` second. In Python `/` is true division and can give a decimal, so the f-string `{a / b:.2f}` rounds the quotient to exactly 2 decimal places as required.

name: P1006 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1006 (Quotient and Remainder): read two integers and print the integer quotient on the first line and the remainder on the second line. (OJ: P1006 — Quotient and Remainder)

explanation: Read `a` and `b`, then use integer division `a // b` for the quotient and modulo `a % b` for the remainder. The two results go on separate lines — quotient first, remainder second — so two `print` calls are needed.

name: P1007 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1007 (Rectangle Perimeter and Area): read the length and width and print the perimeter on the first line and the area on the second line. (OJ: P1007 — Rectangle Perimeter and Area)

explanation: Read the length `a` and width `b`, then compute the perimeter `2 * (a + b)` and the area `a * b`. The parentheses matter: `2 * (a + b)` doubles the sum of the sides, which is the perimeter formula. Perimeter is printed on the first line and area on the second.

name: P1008 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1008 (Circle Circumference and Area): read the radius and print the circumference on the first line and the area on the second line, taking π = 3.14. (OJ: P1008 — Circle Circumference and Area)

explanation: Read the radius `r`, then define `pi = 3.14` before it is used. The circumference is `2 * pi * r` and the area is `pi * r * r`; both are formatted with `:.2f` for two decimals. Every name must be defined above the line that uses it — that is what fixes the order.

name: P1009 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1009 (Power Operation): read the base and the exponent and print the power a raised to b. (OJ: P1009 — Power Operation)

explanation: Read the base `a` and the exponent `b`, then `a ** b` raises `a` to the power `b` (two asterisks mean power in Python). The `print` simply comes last, after both variables exist.

name: P1010 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1010: read a temperature in Celsius and convert it to Fahrenheit using F = C × 9 / 5 + 32. (OJ: P1010 — Fahrenheit to Celsius)

explanation: Read the Celsius temperature `c`, then apply the formula `F = C × 9 / 5 + 32` — multiplication and division happen before the addition, which is Python's normal operator precedence, so no extra parentheses are needed. Finally `print(f"{f:.2f}")` shows the result with two decimals.

name: P1016 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1016 (Absolute Value): read an integer n and print its absolute value. (OJ: P1016 — Absolute Value)

explanation: Read `n`, then flip its sign only when it is negative: the line `n = -n` is indented under `if n < 0:`, so it belongs to the `if` and runs only for negative values. The final `print(n)` sits outside the `if` and outputs the non-negative result in every case.

feature extraction

Pipeline:
1. **Input Image** — the raw picture goes in.
2. **Feature Extraction** — pull out edges, colors and shapes.
3. **Feature Map** — organize the extracted features.
4. **Understanding** — the AI decides what it sees.

name: P1011 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1011 (Arithmetic Sequence Sum): read the first term a1, the common difference d and the number of terms n, then print the n-th term on the first line and the sum of the first n terms on the second line. (OJ: P1011 — Arithmetic Sequence Sum)

explanation: Read `a1`, `d` and `n` first. The n-th term is `an = a1 + (n - 1) * d`, and the sum formula `sn = n * (a1 + an) // 2` needs `an`, so it must come after. The `//` keeps the division exact, since `n * (a1 + an)` is always even. Print `an` on the first line and `sn` on the second.

name: P1012 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1012 (Chickens and Rabbits in a Cage): read the number of heads h and the number of legs l, then print the number of chickens and rabbits — chickens on the first line and rabbits on the second line. (OJ: P1012 — Chickens and Rabbits in a Cage)

explanation: Read the heads `h` and legs `l`. Giving every head 2 legs uses `2 * h` legs, so the extra `l - 2 * h` legs are the rabbits' second pair — halving gives the rabbit count `r = (l - 2 * h) // 2`, and the rest `c = h - r` are chickens. `r` must be computed before `c` because `c` uses it; print `c` then `r`, one per line. The input is guaranteed valid, so no checks are needed.

name: P1013 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1013 (Sum and Average of Three Numbers): read three integers a, b and c, then print their sum on the first line and their average on the second line, rounded to two decimal places. (OJ: P1013 — Sum and Average of Three Numbers)

explanation: Read `a`, `b` and `c`, then `print(a + b + c)` writes the sum on the first line. The average `(a + b + c) / 3` goes on the second line, formatted with `:.2f` to show exactly two decimals. The sum itself prints as a plain integer.

name: P1014 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1014 (Hours, Minutes and Seconds Conversion): read a non-negative integer n (seconds) and print the equivalent hours, minutes and seconds, one per line. (OJ: P1014 — Hours, Minutes and Seconds Conversion)

explanation: Read the total seconds `n`. Hours are `n // 3600` (integer division counts whole hours); the leftover `n % 3600` divided by 60 — again with `//` — gives whole minutes; and `n % 60` is what remains as seconds. Each value goes on its own line through a separate `print`, and all computing happens after `n` is read.

name: P1015 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1015 (Trapezoid Area): read the upper base a, the lower base b and the height h, then print the trapezoid area on one line, rounded to two decimal places. (OJ: P1015 — Trapezoid Area)

explanation: Read the upper base `a`, lower base `b` and height `h`, then apply the trapezoid area formula `(a + b) * h / 2`. The parentheses make the two bases sum before multiplying by the height, and `:.2f` rounds the result to two decimals.

name: 🔢 Ordering: the face registration pipeline

content.text: The second poster shows how registration works. Drag the steps into the correct order.

explanation:
Correct order:
1. **Capture face** — a photo must exist before anything else.
2. **Detect & align** — find the face and straighten it.
3. **Extract features** — compute the face signature from the aligned photo.
4. **Store in database** — save the record for future comparison.
5. **Registration complete** — only after storing.

name: P1017 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1017 (The Larger of Two Numbers): read two integers and print the larger one. (OJ: P1017 — The Larger of Two Numbers)

explanation: Read `a` and `b`, then compare them once: `if a > b:` prints `a`, otherwise the `else` branch prints `b`. The indented lines belong to their `if` / `else`, and exactly one of the two `print` calls runs.

name: P1018 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1018 (Odd or Even): read an integer n and print "Even" if it is even, otherwise "Odd". (OJ: P1018 — Odd or Even)

explanation: Read `n` and test `n % 2 == 0` — the remainder after dividing by 2 tells evenness. Even numbers take the `if` branch and print `Even`; everything else falls into `else` and prints `Odd`. The two indented prints belong to their branch.

name: P1019 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1019 (Pass or Fail): read a score s and print "Pass" if s is at least 60, otherwise "Fail". (OJ: P1019 — Pass or Fail)

explanation: Read the score `s`. The condition `s >= 60` is inclusive — exactly 60 still passes — so `Pass` is printed in the `if` branch and `Fail` in the `else`.

name: P1020 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1020 (Positive, Negative or Zero): read an integer n and print "Positive", "Negative" or "Zero". (OJ: P1020 — Positive, Negative or Zero)

explanation: Read `n` and check the cases top to bottom: `n > 0` prints `Positive`, `elif n < 0` prints `Negative`, and the final `else` catches the only remaining case, `Zero`. `elif` runs only when the previous condition failed, so the three-way chain covers every integer exactly once.

name: P1021 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1021 (Grade Evaluation): read a score s and print its grade A, B, C, D or F. (OJ: P1021 — Grade Evaluation)

options: If s is 90 or more, do the following:
Otherwise, if s is 80 or more, do the following:
Otherwise, if s is 70 or more, do the following:
Otherwise, if s is 60 or more, do the following:
explanation: Read the score `s` and walk the grade ladder from the top: 90 and above is `A`, 80–89 `B`, 70–79 `C`, 60–69 `D`, below 60 `F`. Checking from high to low lets each step be a single comparison like `s >= 80` — the `elif` chain guarantees earlier (higher) ranges were already ruled out, so no compound conditions are needed.

name: P1022 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1022 (Non-zero Check): read an integer n and print "Nonzero" if it is not zero, otherwise "Zero". (OJ: P1022 — Non-zero Check)

explanation: Read `n` and test `n != 0` — `!=` means *not equal*. Non-zero values take the `if` branch and print `Nonzero`; the only remaining value, 0, falls into `else` and prints `Zero`.

name: P1023 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1023 (Point in Rectangle): read a point (x, y) and print "Inside" if it lies inside or on the rectangle [0,10] x [0,10], otherwise "Outside". (OJ: P1023 — Point in Rectangle)

options: if x >= 0 and x <= 10 and y >= 0 and y <= 10:
explanation: Read `x` and `y`. The point is inside the rectangle only when all four bounds hold: `x` between 0 and 10 **and** `y` between 0 and 10. The `and` operator requires every comparison to be true; any failed bound drops into `else` and prints `Outside`.

name: P1024 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1024 (Multiples of 3 or 5): read an integer n and print "Yes" if it is a multiple of 3 or of 5, otherwise "No". (OJ: P1024 — Multiples of 3 or 5)

explanation: Read `n` and test `n % 3 == 0 or n % 5 == 0`. The `or` is true when either side holds, so multiples of 3, of 5, and of both all print `Yes`; every other value prints `No` in the `else`.

name: P1025 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1025 (Triangle Validity and Classification): read three side lengths and print "NotTriangle", "Equilateral", "Isosceles" or "Scalene". (OJ: P1025 — Triangle Validity and Classification)

options: If the sides cannot form a triangle (one side is at least as long as the other two put together):
Otherwise, if all three sides are equal:
Otherwise, if any two sides are equal:
Otherwise, when all three sides are different:
explanation: Read sides `a`, `b` and `c`, and test in priority order. First the triangle inequality: if any side reaches or exceeds the sum of the other two — `a + b <= c or a + c <= b or b + c <= a` — print `NotTriangle`. This must come first, otherwise impossible triples like 1, 1, 5 would slip into a shape branch. Then all sides equal prints `Equilateral`, any two equal prints `Isosceles`, and the rest print `Scalene`. The `if` / `elif` chain stops at the first match, which is exactly this priority.

name: P1031 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1031 (Greatest Common Divisor): read two positive integers a and b and print gcd(a, b). (OJ: P1031 — Greatest Common Divisor)

explanation: Read `a` and `b`, then run Euclid's algorithm: while `b` is not 0, save the remainder `r = a % b`, slide `a = b` and `b = r`. Each round shrinks the pair, and when `b` reaches 0 the gcd sits in `a`, printed after the loop. name: P1032 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1032 (Collatz Steps): read a positive integer n and print how many Collatz steps it needs to reach 1. (OJ: P1032 — Collatz Steps)

explanation: Read `n` and start `steps` at 0. While `n` has not reached 1, the inner `if` / `else` picks the rule — even: `n = n // 2`, odd: `n = 3 * n + 1` — and `steps = steps + 1` runs every round (it is indented at the same level as the `if`). When the loop ends, `steps` holds the answer for the `print`.

name: P1033 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1033 (Reverse a Number): read a non-negative integer n and print its decimal digits reversed. (OJ: P1033 — Reverse a Number)

options: Set the reversed number rev to 0.
While n is greater than 0, repeat these two steps:
Take the last digit of n and add it to the end of rev.
Chop that last digit off n.
explanation: Read `n` and start `rev` at 0. Each round does two things in this exact order: `rev = rev * 10 + n % 10` lifts the last digit of `n` onto the right end of `rev`, then `n = n // 10` drops that digit from `n`. Repeating until `n` is 0 moves all digits over in reverse; the `print` comes after the loop. Swapping the two loop lines would break the digit order.

name: P1035 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1035 (Divisible by k): read two positive integers n and k and print how many times n can be divided by k with no remainder. (OJ: P1035 — Divisible by k)

explanation: Read `n` and `k`, start `count` at 0. As long as `n % k == 0` — `k` still divides `n` evenly — the loop divides `n = n // k` and counts one more division. It stops at the first value `k` no longer divides, and `count` is how many times `k` went in, printed after the loop.

name: P1030 Code Order

content.text: Arrange the lines below into the correct order to solve P1030 (Maximum of n Numbers): read an integer n and then n integers, and print the maximum among them. (OJ: P1030 — Maximum of n Numbers)

options: Read the first number and remember it as best.
For the remaining n − 1 numbers, repeat these three steps:
If x is greater than best:
Remember x as the new best.
explanation: Read `n`, then read the first value straight into `best` — that is why the loop runs only `n - 1` more times. Each round reads the next `x` and keeps `best` only if it is already bigger: `if x > best: best = x`. After the loop, `best` is the maximum. Seeding `best` with the first value also handles all-negative inputs, where starting from 0 would fail.
